fixes.title: Zombie work items — add reaper/timeout mechanism
fixes.problem: When a helper team accepts a help request, the work_item transitions to 'in_progress' and the help_request to 'accepted'. If the helper crashes or hangs, both records stay in those states permanently. No other team can pick up the work because the help_request is no longer 'open'. The system has no timeout or heartbeat mechanism to detect this. Stress tests (TestZombieWorkItems, TestZombieHelpRequests) confirm the issue — they detect zombies via raw SQL but the module provides no API for it.
fixes.location: Class HelpProtocol — new method needed after fulfill_help() (after line 507)
fixes.fix_description: Add a reap_stale_work() method that finds work items stuck in 'in_progress' and help requests stuck in 'accepted' beyond a configurable timeout. Reset them to 'available_for_help'/'open' respectively so they can be reassigned. Also add a configurable STALE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS class attribute.
fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) a work item stuck in 'in_progress' for longer than timeout is reset to 'available_for_help' with assigned_to=NULL, (2) an 'accepted' help request with no resolved_at is reset to 'open' with accepted_by cleared, (3) items within the timeout window are NOT reaped, (4) after reaping, auto_assign can reassign the work.
fixes.risk: If timeout is too aggressive, legitimate slow work could be reaped. Mitigate by making timeout configurable and defaulting to a generous 5 minutes. The reaper should only be called by a coordinator, not by individual teams.

fixes.title: No input validation on update_status() — accepts any string
fixes.problem: update_status() accepts any arbitrary string for the status parameter. The stress test TestInvalidStatusValues confirms that 'TOTALLY_INVALID_STATUS' is stored without error. Invalid statuses break get_idle_teams(), get_busy_teams(), and get_teams_needing_help() because those methods filter on specific status values. A team with status 'banana' would be invisible to all detection queries. The VALID_STATUSES set is defined at line 23 but never used for validation.
fixes.location: update_status() method, lines 221-282. Also affects add_work_item() priority validation.
fixes.fix_description: Add validation at the top of update_status() that checks status against VALID_STATUSES. Also validate progress_pct is within 0-100 range. Add VALID_PRIORITIES constant and validate priority in add_work_item().
fixes.fix_code:
# Add after line 23 (after VALID_STATUSES definition):
VALID_PRIORITIES = {"low", "medium", "high", "critical"}

# Replace update_status method body (lines 241-282) — add validation after docstring:
    @_retry_on_busy
    def update_status(
        self,
        status: str,
        progress_pct: float,
        current_task: str,
        est_completion: Optional[float] = None,
    ) -> None:
        """Update this team's status.

        Parameters
        ----------
        status:
            One of: idle, working, needs_help, helping, complete.
        progress_pct:
            Percentage complete (0-100).
        current_task:
            Description of current task.
        est_completion:
            Estimated completion timestamp (epoch seconds).

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError:
            If status is not a valid status value or progress_pct is out of range.
        """
        self._check_closed()
        if status not in VALID_STATUSES:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Invalid status {status!r}. Must be one of: {', '.join(sorted(VALID_STATUSES))}"
            )
        if not (0 <= progress_pct <= 100):
            raise ValueError(
                f"progress_pct must be between 0 and 100, got {progress_pct}"
            )
        now = time.time()
        with self._lock:
            # Count work items for this team
            row = self._conn.execute(
                "SELECT COUNT(*) as total FROM work_items WHERE team = ?",
                (self.team,),
            ).fetchone()
            total = row["total"] if row else 0

            row = self._conn.execute(
                "SELECT COUNT(*) as done FROM work_items WHERE team = ? AND status = 'completed'",
                (self.team,),
            ).fetchone()
            done = row["done"] if row else 0

            self._conn.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO team_status (team, status, progress_pct, estimated_completion,
                    current_task, work_items_total, work_items_done, last_updated)
                VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(team) DO UPDATE SET
                    status = excluded.status,
                    progress_pct = excluded.progress_pct,
                    estimated_completion = excluded.estimated_completion,
                    current_task = excluded.current_task,
                    work_items_total = excluded.work_items_total,
                    work_items_done = excluded.work_items_done,
                    last_updated = excluded.last_updated
                """,
                (self.team, status, progress_pct, est_completion,
                 current_task, total, done, now),
            )
            self._conn.commit()

        # Publish status-update to bus
        self._publish_bus("global", "info", {
            "event": "status-update",
            "team": self.team,
            "status": status,
            "progress_pct": progress_pct,
            "est_completion": est_completion,
        })

# In add_work_item (line 289), add priority validation after self._check_closed() call:
        self._check_closed()
        if priority not in VALID_PRIORITIES:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Invalid priority {priority!r}. Must be one of: {', '.join(sorted(VALID_PRIORITIES))}"
            )
fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) update_status('banana', ...) raises ValueError, (2) update_status('idle', ...) succeeds, (3) progress_pct=-50 raises ValueError, (4) progress_pct=999 raises ValueError, (5) add_work_item with priority='urgent' raises ValueError. Update existing stress tests TestInvalidStatusValues and TestNegativeProgress to expect ValueError instead of silent acceptance.
fixes.risk: This is a breaking change for any caller currently passing invalid statuses. The stress tests TestInvalidStatusValues and TestNegativeProgress will need to be updated to expect ValueError. Any existing code relying on the lenient behavior will break — but this is the correct behavior.

fixes.title: Bus write failures can crash callers despite docstring claiming fire-and-forget
fixes.problem: The _publish_bus() method has a try/except that catches exceptions and returns None (lines 165-191). However, update_status() at line 276 calls _publish_bus() OUTSIDE the DB lock. The _publish_bus method itself looks correct — it catches all exceptions. BUT the real bug is: request_help() at line 383 calls _publish_bus after the lock is released and passes `json.loads(caps)` inline. If `caps` contains malformed JSON (which could happen from a corrupt DB or bad data), json.loads() raises BEFORE _publish_bus is entered, crashing the caller AFTER the DB commit. The docstring says 'Bus write failures are logged but never propagated' but that is only true inside the method, not for argument preparation outside it.
fixes.location: request_help() method, line 388: json.loads(caps) can throw outside _publish_bus try/except
fixes.fix_description: Wrap the _publish_bus() call sites that do argument computation (especially json.loads) in try/except. Better yet, move the json.loads inside _publish_bus or pre-compute safely. Also add a guard in request_help() around the bus publish call.
fixes.fix_code:
# Replace lines 382-391 in request_help() with:
        # Publish help-request to bus (fire-and-forget)
        try:
            parsed_caps = json.loads(caps) if caps else []
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
            parsed_caps = []
        self._publish_bus("global", "info", {
            "event": "help-request",
            "request_id": request_id,
            "work_item_id": work_item_id,
            "description": description,
            "required_capabilities": parsed_caps,
            "estimated_minutes": est,
        })
fixes.test_needed: Test that request_help() succeeds and returns a valid request_id even when the capabilities JSON stored in the DB is malformed (simulate by directly inserting bad JSON into required_capabilities column).
fixes.risk: Low risk. This is purely defensive. The fix only affects the bus notification path, not the DB commit path.

fixes.title: No authorization on fulfill_help — any team can fulfill any request
fixes.problem: fulfill_help() (lines 487-507) does not check that the calling team is the accepted_by_team for the help request. Any team can call fulfill_help(request_id) and mark it as fulfilled, even if they never accepted it. This means: (1) a team that did not do the work can claim completion, (2) an 'open' request can be marked 'fulfilled' without ever being accepted, (3) an already-fulfilled request can have its resolved_at overwritten. The stress plan (EP-HP-005) identifies this exact gap.
fixes.fix_description: Add authorization check: verify the request exists, is in 'accepted' status, and accepted_by_team matches self.team. Raise ValueError if not authorized.
fixes.fix_code:
# Replace fulfill_help method (lines 486-507):
    @_retry_on_busy
    def fulfill_help(self, request_id: int) -> None:
        """Mark a help request as fulfilled and its work item as completed.

        Only the team that accepted the request can fulfill it.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError:
            If request does not exist, is not in 'accepted' status,
            or was not accepted by this team.
        """
        self._check_closed()
        now = time.time()
        with self._lock:
            row = self._conn.execute(
                "SELECT status, accepted_by_team, work_item_id FROM help_requests WHERE id = ?",
                (request_id,),
            ).fetchone()

            if row is None:
                raise ValueError(f"Help request {request_id} does not exist")
            if row["status"] != "accepted":
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Help request {request_id} is in status {row['status']!r}, expected 'accepted'"
                )
            if row["accepted_by_team"] != self.team:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"Help request {request_id} was accepted by {row['accepted_by_team']!r}, "
                    f"not by {self.team!r}"
                )

            self._conn.execute(
                "UPDATE help_requests SET status = 'fulfilled', resolved_at = ? WHERE id = ?",
                (now, request_id),
            )

            if row["work_item_id"] is not None:
                self._conn.execute(
                    "UPDATE work_items SET status = 'completed', updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?",
                    (now, row["work_item_id"]),
                )

            self._conn.commit()
fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) team-b can fulfill a request it accepted — success, (2) team-c trying to fulfill a request accepted by team-b raises ValueError, (3) fulfilling a nonexistent request raises ValueError, (4) fulfilling an already-fulfilled request raises ValueError, (5) fulfilling an 'open' request raises ValueError.
fixes.risk: Breaking change: existing code calling fulfill_help() from a team other than the acceptor will now fail. The auto_assign_idle_teams() sets accepted_by_agent to 'auto-assign' and accepted_by_team to the helper team name, so fulfill must be called from a HelpProtocol instance with the correct team. The test_full_flow test calls hp_b.fulfill_help(rid) where hp_b accepted — this will continue to work.

fixes.title: TOCTOU race in auto_assign_idle_teams — helper status not verified atomically
fixes.problem: auto_assign_idle_teams() at line 631 calls find_compatible_helpers() which calls get_idle_teams() to find teams with status 'idle'/'complete'. Then at line 648 it does BEGIN IMMEDIATE and assigns the helper. But between get_idle_teams() and BEGIN IMMEDIATE, the helper team may have changed status to 'working' via its own update_status() call. The code at line 687 unconditionally updates the helper's status to 'helping', overwriting whatever status the helper set. Stress test TestRaceStatusAndAutoAssign exercises this but does not assert the absence of overwrites. The stress plan (FM-HP-005, ST-HP-008) documents this as high severity.
fixes.location: auto_assign_idle_teams() method, lines 612-723, specifically the BEGIN IMMEDIATE block at lines 646-721
fixes.fix_description: Inside the BEGIN IMMEDIATE block, after acquiring the transaction lock, verify the helper team is still in 'idle' or 'complete' status before assigning. If the team has changed status, skip to the next candidate helper.

fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) if a helper team changes to 'working' between get_idle_teams() and the BEGIN IMMEDIATE block, the assignment is skipped and the helper's 'working' status is preserved, (2) a different idle team is tried instead, (3) if no helpers remain idle, the request stays open.
fixes.risk: Low risk. The ROLLBACK + continue path is safe. The only subtle issue: if ALL helpers transition away between the check and the claim, the request stays open — which is the correct behavior (no available helpers).

fixes.title: No closed-state tracking on most methods — opaque sqlite3 errors
fixes.problem: The class has _check_closed() and _closed flag (lines 131-140), but only register_capabilities() at line 206 and (implicitly via the lock) close() use _check_closed(). Methods update_status(), add_work_item(), mark_work_available(), complete_work_item(), request_help(), offer_help(), fulfill_help(), get_open_help_requests(), get_idle_teams(), get_busy_teams(), get_teams_needing_help(), find_compatible_helpers(), and auto_assign_idle_teams() do NOT call _check_closed(). The stress test TestOperationsAfterClose passes because sqlite3 raises its own errors, but the error messages are opaque ('Cannot operate on a closed database') instead of the clear RuntimeError('Connection is closed'). Furthermore, close() can race with operations on other threads.
fixes.location: _check_closed() at lines 137-140; missing from all methods except register_capabilities()
fixes.fix_description: Add self._check_closed() call at the top of every public method, BEFORE acquiring self._lock. This ensures a clear error message. Also ensure close() is idempotent (safe to call twice).
fixes.fix_code:

# Make close() idempotent — replace lines 142-146:
    def close(self) -> None:
        """Close the database connection. Safe to call multiple times."""
        with self._lock:
            if self._closed:
                return
            self._closed = True
            self._conn.close()
fixes.test_needed: Test that after close(): (1) every public method raises RuntimeError (not sqlite3.ProgrammingError), (2) double close() does not raise, (3) the error message is 'Connection is closed'. Update TestOperationsAfterClose to assert RuntimeError specifically.
fixes.risk: Low risk. This is purely additive defensive code. The _check_closed() call is outside the lock so there is a tiny TOCTOU window where close() could be called between _check_closed() and lock acquisition, but the worst case is the existing sqlite3 error rather than our clean RuntimeError — still an improvement.

fixes.title: _retry_on_busy uses fragile string matching instead of error codes
fixes.problem: The _retry_on_busy decorator at line 92 checks `'locked' in str(e).lower() or 'busy' in str(e).lower()` to decide whether to retry. This is fragile: (1) error message wording could change in a future SQLite or Python version, (2) a disk error message that happens to contain the word 'busy' would be incorrectly retried, (3) it doesn't distinguish SQLITE_BUSY (5) from SQLITE_LOCKED (6) which may need different handling. Python 3.11+ exposes sqlite_errorcode on the exception object. The stress plan EP-HP-004 identifies this.
fixes.fix_description: Check sqlite3.OperationalError's sqlite_errorcode attribute (Python 3.11+) for SQLITE_BUSY (5) and SQLITE_LOCKED (6). Fall back to string matching for older Python versions.
fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) SQLITE_BUSY errors trigger retries (existing concurrent tests cover this), (2) non-busy OperationalErrors (e.g., 'disk I/O error') are raised immediately without retry, (3) the _is_busy_or_locked helper correctly identifies busy/locked errors by code when available.
fixes.risk: Low risk. The fallback to string matching preserves existing behavior for older Python versions. The error code check is strictly more correct.

fixes.title: Empty list [] treated as falsy for required_caps — stores None instead of '[]'
fixes.problem: In add_work_item() at line 299: `caps_json = json.dumps(required_caps) if required_caps else None`. Because Python treats empty list `[]` as falsy, passing `required_caps=[]` stores None in the database instead of the JSON string '[]'. This means there is no way to distinguish 'no capabilities specified' (None) from 'explicitly no capabilities required' ([]). The stress test test_empty_required_caps_work_item confirms this behavior and documents it as a known issue. Downstream, find_compatible_helpers() treats both None and '[]' the same way (line 594: returns all idle teams), so the semantic difference is currently moot — but it's still data loss.
fixes.fix_description: Change the condition to check `is not None` instead of truthiness, so that `[]` is stored as '[]' in the database.
fixes.fix_code:
# Replace line 299:
# Old:
        caps_json = json.dumps(required_caps) if required_caps else None
# New:
        caps_json = json.dumps(required_caps) if required_caps is not None else None
fixes.test_needed: Test that: (1) add_work_item(required_caps=[]) stores '[]' in DB, not None, (2) add_work_item(required_caps=None) stores None, (3) add_work_item(required_caps=['coding']) stores '["coding"]'. Update test_empty_required_caps_work_item to assert row['required_capabilities'] == '[]'.
fixes.risk: Low risk. This changes stored data for the empty-list case from None to '[]'. Downstream json.loads('[]') returns [] which behaves identically to the current code path where None is treated as empty. The only risk is if external consumers of the DB depend on the None representation for empty lists.

chokepoints.description: auto_assign_idle_teams() is a serial bottleneck. It iterates open requests one by one (line 629), and for each request calls find_compatible_helpers() (line 631) which itself calls get_idle_teams() (line 592). Each of these is a separate DB query that acquires and releases self._lock. For N open requests and M idle teams, this is O(N * M) database queries. With 100 open requests and 50 idle teams, this means ~200+ lock acquisitions and DB queries in a single auto_assign call. The stress test TestHighConcurrencyAutoAssign shows this working but at significant latency.
chokepoints.solution: Prefetch all data in a single query at the start: get all open requests with their capabilities, all idle teams with their capabilities, then do the matching in Python. Only hit the DB for the BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim. This reduces DB queries from O(N*M) to O(N) (one per assignment attempt plus 2 initial queries).
chokepoints.impact: Expected 5-10x speedup for auto_assign with many open requests. Reduces lock contention significantly, improving concurrent throughput.

chokepoints.description: Every call to update_status() runs two COUNT(*) queries (lines 244-254) to count total and completed work items for the team, even though these counts are only informational metadata in team_status. Under 50 concurrent teams each calling update_status() frequently (stress test ST-HP-003 does 50 teams x 100 updates = 5000 calls), these redundant COUNT queries double the DB load. The counts could be maintained incrementally or computed lazily.
chokepoints.solution: Option A: Remove the COUNT queries from update_status() and compute them lazily only when reading team_status. Option B: Maintain the counts incrementally in add_work_item() and complete_work_item() instead of recomputing on every status update. Option A is simpler and eliminates the bottleneck entirely.
chokepoints.impact: Halves the number of DB queries in update_status(), the most frequently called method. Expected 30-50% throughput improvement under concurrent status updates.

chokepoints.description: find_compatible_helpers() calls get_idle_teams() (line 592) which joins team_status with team_capabilities and uses GROUP_CONCAT. Then it iterates through all idle teams in Python doing set intersection (lines 600-606). This could be done in a single SQL query with proper JOINs, avoiding the transfer of all idle team data into Python and the Python-side set operations.
chokepoints.solution: Replace the two-step approach with a single SQL query that joins help_requests, team_capabilities, and team_status, counting matching capabilities directly in SQL. Return only teams with at least one matching capability, pre-sorted by match score.
chokepoints.impact: Eliminates one DB round-trip per call and reduces Python-side processing. Most impactful when there are many idle teams but few with matching capabilities.

chokepoints.description: Every bus write does os.makedirs(self.bus_dir, exist_ok=True) at line 182, even though the directory was likely already created on the first call or in __init__. os.makedirs involves a stat() syscall on every path component. Under high-frequency status updates (50 teams updating repeatedly), this is thousands of unnecessary syscalls.
chokepoints.solution: Cache a flag indicating the bus directory has been created. Check the flag before calling os.makedirs. Set the flag after the first successful makedirs call. Use a class-level or instance-level set to track created directories.
chokepoints.impact: Eliminates one unnecessary syscall per bus write. Minor but measurable under high-frequency workloads.

chokepoints.description: offer_help() and auto_assign_idle_teams() use manual BEGIN IMMEDIATE / COMMIT / ROLLBACK transaction management with nested try/except blocks. This pattern is repeated in both methods with subtle differences. The manual transaction management is error-prone (line 428-429 catches OperationalError on BEGIN but re-raises it, making it indistinguishable from other OperationalErrors). A context manager or helper would reduce code duplication and prevent transaction leaks.
chokepoints.solution: Create a _begin_immediate() context manager that handles BEGIN IMMEDIATE, COMMIT on success, and ROLLBACK on exception. This replaces ~20 lines of boilerplate per method with a single 'with self._begin_immediate():' block. Reduces the surface area for transaction management bugs.
chokepoints.impact: Code quality improvement. Reduces risk of transaction leaks (forgotten ROLLBACK). Makes adding new transactional methods safer.
